item.title: Setting up a virtual machine with Windows
item.description:
Here is my step-by-step procedure for using VMware Workstation to create a Windows 11 guest VM.

Prepare Host

  • Obtain a Windows ISO image and a Windows Product Key.
    • Since I work as a Software Engineer, I have access to those via Visual Studio Benefits (formerly MSDN.)
  • If the host is Windows 11, go to Turn Windows Features on or off and disable everything virtualization-related.

Create the Virtual Machine

  • VMware Workstation → New Virtual Machine...

  • Type of configuration: → Typical (recommended)

  • Install from: → Installer disc image file (iso):

    • Select the previously downloaded ISO image.

  • Virtual machine name: → 'Windows 11'

  • Location: → Enter a location in the host

    • For example 'D:\virtual-machines\windows11'

  • What to encrypt: → only the files needed to support a virtual TPM

  • Encrypted Virtual Machine Password:

    • Enter a good password and note it somewhere.
    • IMPORTANT: Do NOT remember the password for this virtual machine in Credential Manager!

  • Maximum disk size (GB): → '128'

  • Split virtual disk into multiple files → Check

  • Customize Hardware...

    • Memory: → '32768' MB (That's 32 GB; my host has twice that.)
    • Number of processors: → '2'
    • Number of cores per processor: → '8'

  • VM → Settings → Options → Advanced

    • Enable side channel mitigations for Hyper-V enabled hosts → Uncheck
      • (On second thought, this is probably unnecessary, because we have already disabled Hyper-V on the host.)

  • Strangely enough, last time I followed these instructions I was not asked whether I want Secure boot, and I did not check it, and Windows 11 had no problem with that.

Install Windows

  • Note that at any moment during installation:
    • Shift+F10 brings up a command prompt.
    • Ctrl+Alt releases mouse capture from the VM so you can interact with the host.
  • Note for next time: when prompted to select regional format, select English (World). This is rumored to reduce bloatware.
  • Select Image → Windows 11 Pro N
  • Let's connect you to a network → Next
  • Name your device
    • Pick a device name and note it somewhere.
  • How would you like to set up this device?
    • Set up for work or school (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
  • Let's set things up for your work or school
    • Sign-in options → Domain join instead (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
  • Who's going to use this device?
    • Select a user name and note it somewhere.
  • Create a super memorable password
    • Select a password and note it somewhere.
  • VM → Settings... → Options → Autologin → Activate
    • Enter previously selected user name and password
  • Now add security questions
    • Pick any 3 questions; for each question:
      • In the answer box, just type some random letters. (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
  • Choose privacy settings for your device
    • Uncheck EVERYTHING
    • Click Accept (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)

Configure Windows

  • Settings → System → Display → Scale
    • Change from 100% to 150%
  • Settings → System → Power → Screen and sleep timeouts
    • Plugged in
      • Turn my screen off after → Never
      • Make my device sleep after → Never

Activate Windows

  • Settings → System → Activation
    • Ignore red text (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
    • Click Change product key
      • Enter product key.

Personalize Windows

  • Settings → Personalization
    • Select a theme to apply → Select something nice and dark
    • Background → Personalize your background → Solid color
      • Custom colors View colors → Select something nice and dark
    • Colors → Choose your mode → Dark
    • Accent color → Choose some color that is:
      • Different from the host,
      • Different from other virtual machines.

Enable BitLocker

  • Right-click on DVD drive
    • Disconnect
  • Control Panel → Manage BitLocker
    • Click Turn on BitLocker
    • How do you want to back up your recovery key? → Save to a file
      • Save the file inside the VM
    • Open the file and note somewhere the Computer Identifier and the Recovery Key.
    • Choose how much of your drive to encrypt → Encrypt used disk space only
    • Choose which encryption mode to use → New encryption mode
    • Bitlocker system check → Skip.

Take a Snapshot

  • VM → Snapshot → Take Snapshot
    • Name: After BitLocker

Further Configuration

  • Install VMware Tools

    • VM → Install VMware Tools

  • Setup network

    • This is necessary in order to be able to see Shared Folders as drive letters.
    • Settings → Network & Internet
      • Properties (Public network)  → Private network
      • Advanced network settings → Advanced sharing settings
      • File and printer sharing → Check

  • Setup shared folders

    • VM → Settings... → Options → Shared Folders
      • Always enabled → Check
      • Map as a network drive →Check
      • Add...
        • Host path: → 'D:'
        • Name: → 'HostDriveDRoot'

For instructions on how to proceed after that, see Setting up Windows.

item.title: How to organize a Visual Studio Solution
item.description:
Visual Studio is a capricious product, and its "Solution" subsystem is especially capricious. When you look at what options are available you might think you have a great degree of freedom to structure things the way you want, but as you will inevitably (and painfully) find out later, many things have to be done in precisely one, entirely undocumented way, or else there will be pain of the worst kind: Visual Studio will malfunction either without any error message, or with error messages that are completely unhelpful for locating and fixing the problem.

Here is a list of things I have (painfully) found out over the years.

(Useful pre-reading: About these papers)

The project directory structure must be entirely flat.

All project files must reside in directories that are immediate sub-directories of the solution directory. When adding a project you are given the freedom to put it in a directory anywhere you want, but if you don't put it in a directory exactly under the solution directory, you are going to run into trouble later.

If you have hundreds of projects, and you are thinking that putting them all in one directory is insane, welcome to the Microsoft world, where insane is the order of the day.

From within Visual Studio, you can create what Microsoft calls "Solution Folders" to arrange your projects in a hierarchy at least within Visual Studio's "Solution Explorer" panel, but even this has a caveat, keep reading.

The startup project must be listed first in the solution file.

Solution files are, luckily, text files. Solution files with the .sln extension are in a ridiculous ad-hoc format consisting of, among other things, entries delimited with "Project" and "EndProject" and making use of GUIDs to discourage anyone from touching it or even looking at it. Luckily they have now introduced .slnx files, which are a bit more lean, but they are now in XML, (Microsoft seems to be stuck in the 1980's,) so they are still far more verbose than necessary, and they still contain GUIDs here and there. Regardless of the file format, you are free to edit the solution file and re-order these entries in any way you like, and it seems to have absolutely no effect because the Visual Studio Solution Explorer will sort them alphabetically anyway, but there is one kind of re-ordering that you can do which actually matters: The entry which stands for your startup project must be the first entry.

If you do not do this, then each time you delete the .vs directory, restart Visual Studio, and try to launch your solution, you will be greeted with the all too familiar, extremely annoying, and extremely stupid message which says that you cannot launch a project which builds a library instead of an executable. This is happening because when the .vs directory is deleted, Visual Studio forgets the startup project, and when Visual Studio is launched with no startup project configured it absolutely has to establish a startup project, and it absolutely has to do this automatically, without asking you. In doing so, it picks the first project that it finds in the solution file, and it is not smart enough to skip projects that build libraries instead of executables.

The startup project must not be nested in a solution folder.

As mentioned earlier, you can use "Solution Folders" to arrange your projects in a hierarchy; however, the project that you usually want to have as the startup project must not be nested in a solution folder, it must be placed right under the root node of the solution.

If you nest your startup project in a solution folder, then Visual Studio will again, entirely capriciously, ignore it when automatically selecting a project as the startup project each time you delete the .vs directory.

Test projects must be given names that end in " Test". (Yes, that is a space.)

Usually, projects come in pairs: there is a production project, and a test project. Usually, we give the test project the same name as the production project, with a suitable suffix to indicate that this is a test project. If your production project is called "Covfefe", you might think that you have plenty of options to call your test project: "CovfefeTest", "Covfefe.Test", "Covfefe-Test", "Covfefe_Test", etc. Actually, none of these will work. You have to call it "Covfefe Test", with a space before "Test".

This is because the Visual Studio Solution Explorer uses different sorting rules from Windows File Explorer, so if you use anything but " Test" as a suffix for test projects you will find your projects listed in a different order between the Solution Explorer and the File Explorer. Depending on what you choose, your test projects will appear either before or after your production projects, either in Solution Explorer or in File Explorer, but not in both. The only trick I have been able to find which causes the test projects to always be listed after the production projects both in Solution Explorer and in File Explorer is to make each test project name consist of the production project name suffixed with " Test" (with a space.)

Aaaand, of course, even with this, there is a catch: if you name your projects as I suggested, they will appear in the wrong order when viewing your solution directory on GitHub. Because GitHub uses yet different sorting rules. So, there is no way to achieve a consistent look both in Windows File Explorer, and Visual Studio Solution Explorer, and GitHub.

Solution items must be placed in a custom "_Solution Items" folder.

Solution-level items are a fiasco to begin with; they only exist because the Visual Studio Solution Explorer capriciously hides solution-level files from the user. Instead, Visual Studio offers the "Solution Items" workaround, which is a solution folder under the solution node where you can manually place links to solution-level files that you want to be able to access. (Because having to manually create links to your own files so that you can access them is always fun.)

The default name that Visual Studio gives to this folder is "Solution Items". The first thing you must do with it is to rename it to "_Solution Items", so that it will be sorted first in the list, otherwise it will be hidden among other solution folders.

Old comments

  • Anonymous 2024-12-27 16:05:14 UTC

    Thank you for sharing your experiences and all the useful info. Visual Studio is increasingly becoming such a bloatware, while still missing quite a lot of basic fundamental functionality.

item.title: [SOLVED] Windows: Sound becomes distorted after 1 second of playback
item.description:
So today I started encountering a very weird audio issue: When I play music, it sounds normal in the beginning, but then after about a second the sound gets distorted, as if it is muffled, or as if it is undergoing severe lossy compression. If I stop and resume the music, it goes through the same.

Normally I would know what to do in this situation, but as the years pass Microsoft keeps changing Windows, in the direction of making them dumber and dumber, so in Windows 10 I cannot find the old sound options dialog that I used to use to fix this problem.

Looking around the interwebz for a solution was not easy, so I decided to document the solution that I found. If you are a power user, you can skim through the text and only look at the words in bold-italics.

  1. Type Win+R and type mmsys.cpl. This will bring up the good old sound options, which Microsoft recently made inaccessible by any means other than this magical incantation, because obviously, nobody should ever want to fix any sound problems, because obviously, Windows has no sound problems.
  2. In the Playback tab, locate your Speakers. If you are playing music at that moment, they are easy to locate from the live volume meter right next to them.
  3. Select Properties on your speakers. (Not Configure, but Properties.) This should open a Speakers Properties dialog.
  4. On the Speaker Properties dialog, select the Advanced tab.
  5. Near the bottom of the Advanced tab there is an Enable Fucked Up Sound checkbox, which is actually labelled Enable Enhancements. (Euphemism has always been Microsoft's forte.)
  6. Uncheck that checkbox; you are done.

Afterword

I probably started experiencing this problem right after pairing a new bluetooth sound device. Apparently when Windows detects a new sound device it sets some things up for it, and while doing that it entirely arbitrarily also goes and resets some settings for existing devices, e.g. it enables this "Enhancements" setting for my existing speakers.

item.title: Setting up Windows
item.description:
Instructions for future reference.

Initial Windows configuration

  • Taskbar:

    • Unpin everything. (File explorer, Microsoft edge, Microsoft Store, "Mail", etc.)

    • Right-click → Taskbar settings → Settings / Personalization / Taskbar

      • Search → Hide
      • Task view → Off
      • Widgets → Off
      • Taskbar behaviors
        • Taskbar alignment → Left
        • Show my taskbar on all displays → Enable
      • Replace Command Prompt with Windows PowerShell in the menu when I right-click the start button or press Windows logo key + X → DISABLE
      • Show taskbar buttons on
        • SELECT Main taskbar and taskbar where window is open
      • Show news and interests on the taskbar → DISABLE

    • This does not work anymore in Windows 11:

      • Open the Run Prompt (with Win+R)
      • Execute this nonsense:
        • explorer shell:::{05d7b0f4-2121-4eff-bf6b-ed3f69b894d9}
      • Always show all icons and notifications on the taskbar → ENABLE

  • Enable Developer Mode.

  • Set up user environment variables

    • DIRCMD = /OGNE
    • TEMP = %UserProfile%\AppData\Local\Temp
    • TMP = %UserProfile%\AppData\Local\Temp
    • TMPDIR = %UserProfile%\AppData\Local\Temp

  • Kill let's finish setting up your device. (Might be irrelevant in Windows 11)

    • Go to Settings → System → Notifications → Additional Settings
    • Show the Windows welcome experience after updates and when signed in to show what's new and suggested → DISABLE
    • Suggest ways to get the most out of Windows and finish setting up this device → DISABLE
    • Get tips and suggestions when using Windows → DISABLE

  • Disable Windows Error Reporting

    • Open Edit group policy (gpedit.msc)
    • Go to Local computer Policy → Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows Error Reporting
    • Set Disable Windows Error Reporting to Enabled.

  • Uninstall crapware:

    • Clipchamp - Video Editor (Windows 11)
    • Cortana (Windows 10)
    • Feedback Hub
    • Mail and Calendar
    • Maps
    • Microsoft News (Windows 11)
    • Microsoft OneDrive
    • Microsoft To Do (Windows 11)
    • Movies & TV
    • Office
    • People (Windows 10)
    • Power Automate (Windows 11)
    • Quick Assist (Windows 11)
    • Solitaire Collection / Microsoft Solitaire Collection
    • Sticky Notes
    • Tips (Windows 11)
    • Weather

  • If the computer has been set-up by an organization:

    • Kill RegisteredOrganization
      • Locate the following registry keys and make sure they are empty:
        • HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\RegisteredOrganization
        • HKLM\Software\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\RegisteredOrganization

Install software

  • Install Obsidian

    • From https://obsidian.md/

  • Install Hugo

    • In a command prompt, execute:
      • winget install -e --id Hugo.Hugo.Extended

  • Install Sumatra PDF

    • From https://www.sumatrapdfreader.org

  • Install InkScape

    • From https://inkscape.org

  • Install Foobar2000

    • From https://www.foobar2000.org
    • Also install the free encoder pack from https://www.foobar2000.org/encoderpack

  • Install VLC

    • From https://www.videolan.org

  • Install Ditto

    • From https://ditto-cp.sourceforge.io/
    • (because Windows built-in Clipboard History is lame beyond words.)

  • Install 7-Zip

    • From https://www.7-zip.org

  • Install Firefox

    • From https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/

  • Install Notepad++

    • From https://notepad-plus-plus.org/

  • Install AutoHotkey

    • From https://www.autohotkey.com/
    • In case of antivirus trouble, download as a zip file.

  • Install Git

    • Execute winget install Git.Git
    • Or download from https://git-scm.com/downloads/win
    • Under Select Components check Windows Explorer integration / Open Git Bash here
    • Under Choosing the default editor used by Git select Use Notepad++ as Git's default editor.

  • Install TortoiseGit

    • From https://tortoisegit.org/

  • Install Visual Studio Community Edition

    • From https://visualstudio.microsoft.com

  • Install SysInternals Process Explorer

    • From https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/process-explorer
    • Download into %UserProfile%\bin\ProcessExplorer

  • Install a Windows File Explorer extension for SVGs. Either:

    • SVG Preview
      • Via winget install SickSartori.SvgPreview
      • See (https://github.com/SickSartori/svg-preview
      • This is the recommended tool to install.
    • SVG See
      • Via winget install -e --id SVGExplorerExtension.SVGExplorerExtension
      • a.k.a. "SVG Viewer Extension for Windows Explorer"
      • a.k.a." SVG Explorer Extension" by tibold
      • See https://www.free-codecs.com/guides/how-to-preview-svg-files-in-file-explorer.htm
      • See https://github.com/tibold/svg-explorer-extension/releases
      • Pros: "does not add system tray bloat" Cons: "Not maintained anymore"
    • Windows PowerToys
      • Via winget install --id Microsoft.PowerToys --source winget
      • WARNING: heavyweight installation
    • ThioJoe's SVG Thumbnail Extension
      • Via winget install ThioJoe.SvgThumbnailExtension
      • See https://github.com/ThioJoe/win-svg-thumbs-rust

  • Install Opera

    • from https://www.opera.com
    • Install DarkReader from the Google Chrome Store
    • Install Ublock Origin from https://addons.opera.com/en/extensions/details/ublock/

  • Install KeePassXC

    • in PowerShell, execute:
      • powershell winget install --id KeePassXCTeam.KeePassXC -e --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements --disable-interactivity

  • Install Syncthing

    • in PowerShell, execute:

      • powershell winget install --id Syncthing.Syncthing -e --accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements --disable-interactivity

    • Syncthing is installed as a portable zip, so winget puts a link to it at %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\WinGet\Links\syncthing.exe; the shortcut below points at that link, so it survives upgrades.

    • Make Syncthing start hidden on login, and start it now; in PowerShell, execute:

    $link = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Microsoft\WinGet\Links\syncthing.exe"
$s = (New-Object -ComObject WScript.Shell).CreateShortcut("$([Environment]::GetFolderPath('Startup'))\Syncthing.lnk")
$s.TargetPath = $link
$s.Arguments = "serve --no-console --no-browser"
$s.WindowStyle = 7
$s.Save()
Start-Process $link -ArgumentList "serve","--no-console","--no-browser" -WindowStyle Hidden
    • Verify that Syncthing is running; in PowerShell, execute:
    Get-Process syncthing
(Invoke-WebRequest http://127.0.0.1:8384 -UseBasicParsing).StatusCode
    • The second command should print 200.

  • Note:

    • On Windows 10, certain crapware like Game Bar, Mixed Reality Portal, Phone Link, Tips etc. cannot be uninstalled. (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
    • On Windows 11, certain crapware like Microsoft Store, Microsoft Edge, Cortana, Get Help, People, Windows Security, and Your Phone cannot be uninstalled. (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)

More Windows configuration

  • Configure Windows File Explorer

    • Folder Options:
      • General:
        • Open File Explorer to:
          • SELECT This PC
      • View:
        • Files and Folders:
          • Decrease space between items (compact view) → ENABLE (Win11?)
          • Display the full path in the title bar → DISABLE
          • Hidden files and folders → SELECT Show hidden files, folders, and drives
          • Hide extensions for known file types → DISABLE
          • Hide protected operating system files (Recommended) → DISABLE
          • Launch folder windows in a separate process → ENABLE
          • Restore previous folder windows at log-on → ENABLE
        • Apply to Folders → CLICK
    • Right-click in the empty space in the left sidebar (Navigation pane)
      • Show all folders → ENABLE
      • Expand to current folder → ENABLE

  • Disable widgets

    • Settings → Personalization → Lock screen
      • Lock screen status → None

  • Configure Privacy

    • Settings → Privacy & Security
      • Show search highlights → DISABLE
    • In Registry Editor
      • visit HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer\
        • set registry value DisableSearchBoxSuggestions as a DWORD of 1
      • sign out and back in.
    • In GPedit.msc
      • visit User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → File Explorer
        • Turn off display of recent search entries in the File Explorer search box. → DISABLE.

  • Configure Language

    • Settings → Language
      • Preferred languages
        • Add a language
          • English (United States) → ADD
            • Install Language Pack → ENABLE
        • Add a language
          • Ελληνικά (Greek) → ADD
            • Install language pack → DISABLE
            • Text-to-speech → DISABLE
            • Handwriting → DISABLE
      • Windows display language
        • SELECT English (United States)
      • Related settings
        • Administrative language settings → Formats
          • Format: → SELECT English (United States)
          • Short date: → SELECT yyyy-MM-dd
          • Long date: → SELECT dddd, MMMM, d, yyyy
          • Short time: → SELECT HH:mm
          • Long time: → SELECT HH:mm:ss
      • Typing (Spelling, typing, and keyboard settings)
        • Autocorrect misspelled words →DISABLE

  • Configure Accessibility

    • Settings → Accessibility →
      • Visual effects
        • Dismiss notifications after this amount of time → SELECT 5 minutes (the maximum)
      • Text cursor
        • Text cursor thickness → SELECT 2
      • Keyboard
        • Use Sticky Keys
          • Allow the shortcut key to start Sticky Keys → DISABLE
        • Use Toggle Keys
          • Allow the shortcut key to start Toggle Keys → DISABLE
        • Use Filter Keys
          • Allow the shortcut key to start Filter Keys → DISABLE
        • Change how keyboard shortcuts work
          • Underline access keys when available → ENABLE

  • Personalize

    • Settings → Accounts
      • Your Info → Create your picture → Browse for one
        • Save and browse for this picture:

  • Settings → Personalization

    • Background
    • Βackground → SELECT Picture
    • Choose a photo → Download, browse to, and select one of the following images:
    • Choose a fit for your desktop image → SELECT Tile - Colors - Choose your color → SELECT Dark - Choose your accent color → SELECT Custom color, make it orange, medium brightness. - Show accent color on the following surfaces - Start, taskbar, and action center → ENABLE - Title bars and window borders → ENABLE
    • Fix the title-bar color of inactive windows
      • Using RegEdit, navigate to:
        • HKEY\_CURRENT\_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\DWM
      • set the DWORD value AccentColorInactive to 2f2f2f. (Add the value if missing.)
    • Start
      • Show suggestions occasionally in Start → DISABLE - System →
    • Multi-tasking → Alt + Tab
      • Pressing Alt + Tab shows
        • SELECT Open windows only
    • Shared experiences
      • Share across devices → DISABLE - Clipboard →
    • Clipboard history → DISABLE - Create an Administrator Command Prompt shortcut
    • Search for Command Prompt
    • Create a shortcut on the desktop
    • Edit properties
    • Select Advanced
    • Select Run as Administrator
    • Pin to start - Create an Administrator Powershell shortcut
    • Search for Powershell
    • Create a shortcut on the desktop
    • Edit properties
    • Select Advanced
    • Select Run as Administrator
    • Pin to start - Create a shortcut to Services
    • Search for Services
    • Pin to start - Create a shortcut to RegEdit
    • Search for RegEdit
    • Pin to start - Create a shortcut to CharMap
    • Search for CharMap
    • Pin to start

  • Unfuck Windows

    • Disable application pinning to taskbar
      • Run gpedit.msc
      • Go to User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Start menu and Taskbar
      • Look for Do not allow pinning programs to the Taskbar → Enable it.
    • Disable fucking up of the Alt+Tab switcher
      • Open windows settings (Win+I)
      • Search for multitasking settings
      • Find Show tabs from apps when snapping or pressing Alt+Tab
        • → set to Don't show tabs

  • Enable natural mouse wheel scrolling

    • Follow the instructions at Mouse Wheel Natural Scrolling in Windows

  • If dealing with Nazi admins from hell who have taken control over your HOMEDRIVE and HOMEPATH variables and forced them to point to some network drive, thus preventing you from using SSH unless connected to their stupid network:

    • Add the following environment variable:
      • HOME = %UserProfile%

  • Configure Memory Compression

    • In an ELEVATED PowerShell prompt, execute the following:
      • Disable-MMAgent -mc

  • Configure UAC

    • Go to Settings, search for UAC, select User Account Control Settings, set slider to Never notify.
      • Justification: In principle the UAC notification is a good thing to have, but Windows is so fucked up that the UAC notification often starts minimized in the taskbar instead of full screen, so it does not get noticed.

  • Install fonts needed for editing the blog

    • Install only the static fonts (the files in the static folder of each download), never the variable ones (*-VariableFont_*.ttf).
      • Justification: Inkscape stores the weight chosen for a variable font as a variation (font-variation-settings), which Chromium (Chrome, Obsidian) ignores for installed fonts, so the same SVG looks different in Inkscape and in Obsidian.
    • Download Anton from https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Anton
      • Right-click Anton-Regular.ttf → Install
    • Download Bitter from https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Bitter
      • Select all files in static → right-click → Install
    • Download Noto Sans from https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Noto+Sans
      • Select all files in static → right-click → Install
    • Download Noto Sans Mono from https://fonts.google.com/noto/specimen/Noto+Sans+Mono
      • Select all files in static → right-click → Install
    • Download EB Garamond from https://fonts.google.com/specimen/EB+Garamond
      • Select all files in static → right-click → Install

Configure applications

  • Configure Ditto

    • ... → Quick Options
      • Lines per clip → SELECT 1
      • View Caption Bar On → SELECT Top
    • Options
      • Keyboard Shortcuts
        • Activate Ditto (2) → SET Win+V
          • This will not work because starting with Windows 10 Microsoft has reserved all Win keys for its own use -- FUCK YOU MICROSOFT.
        • Activate Ditto (2) → SET Ctrl+`
        • Move clips to the top of the list on paste → ENABLE

  • Configure 7-Zip

    • Options
      • 7-Zip tab:
        • Icons in context menu → ENABLE
        • Context menu items:
          • DISABLE ALL, then:
            • Open Archive → ENABLE
            • Extract to \<Folder> → ENABLE
            • `Add to <Archive>.zip → ENABLE
      • Settings tab:
        • Show real file icons → ENABLE

  • Configure Firefox

    • Visit about:config and set browser.tabs.tabMinWidth to 50
    • install Dark Reader extension
    • install UBlock Origin extension
    • install Markdown Viewer extension by simov
      • Options → allow all file access, allow all site access
      • Theme → Water-Dark

  • Configure Google Chrome

    • Stop Chrome from nagging to be made the default browser:
      • Right-click the Chrome shortcut → Properties → Shortcut tab
      • Target: → append --no-default-browser-check
    • Disable background tasks: (FUCK YOU GOOGLE)
      • Go to chrome://settings/system
        • Continue running background apps when Google Chrome is closed → DISABLE.

  • Configure Git

    • Add C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin to the PATH environment variable so that bash is in the path.

  • Configure TortoiseGit

    • Select all defaults, except:
      • English (GB) dictionary → DISABLE
      • SSH → SELECT OpenSSH (Alternatively, after installing, go to Options → Network → SSH → SSH client: and enter C:\Windows\System32\OpenSSH\ssh.exe`)
    • Settings → Colors 1 → Dark Theme → ENABLE
    • Select any two files in Windows File Explorer
    • Right-click on the files → TortoiseGit → Diff → File → Settings → Colors → Use dark mode → ENABLE

  • Configure SysInternals Process Explorer

    • Options
      • Run At Logon → ENABLE
      • Hide When Minimized` → ENABLE
      • Allow Only One Instance → ENABLE
      • Confirm Kill → DISABLE
      • Tray Icons → Commit History → ENABLE

  • Configure Visual Studio

    • Extensions → Installed
      • Remove pre-installed crap. (FUCK YOU MICROSOFT)
    • Tools → Import and Export Settings... → Import and Export Settings Wizard

item.title: How to ALWAYS show all icons on the Windows 11 taskbar
item.description:
2026 UPDATE: This does not work anymore. It may have worked under Windows 10 and for a while under Windows 11, but starting from about the middle of 2026 it does nohing.

To always show all system tray icons in Windows 11:

Open the Run prompt (Win+R) and execute the following nonsense:

explorer shell:::{05d7b0f4-2121-4eff-bf6b-ed3f69b894d9}

In the dialog that appears, there will be a checkbox to always show all icons and notifications on the taskbar.

Original source of information: TheWindowsClub

<rant-mode>

As always, with Windows 11 Microsoft is continuing its long tradition of trying to force upon everyone their own very specific ways of doing things, which range from retarded to fully retarded. Casual users and new users might not know the difference, but every single old power user on the planet is likely to get pissed off.

And as usual, when they change things, they follow the creeping approach:

  • Windows 95 supported taskbar icons: if an application had a taskbar icon, then the icon would appear on the taskbar, simple as that.
  • Windows XP allowed you to choose to hide some icons. Okay, whatever.
  • Windows 7 started only showing the taskbar icons of Microsoft applications and hiding icons from anyone else by default 1, but at least the option to always show all taskbar icons was easy to reach.
  • Windows 10 required you to go digging into settings to find the option to show taskbar icons from others.
  • Now, with Windows 11 this option is not available anymore, at least not without magical incantations like the one shown here.
  • Judging by the obvious trend, the next version of windows will require launching RegEdit to fix this.

</rant-mode>

  1. Note that for that move they should have been sued to non-existence, but they were not, because 'murica, and because complacency. ↩︎

item.title: Mouse Wheel Natural Scrolling in Windows
item.description:
Some time ago and for about a year I used a Mac, which had natural scrolling by default. I decided to resist the urge to immediately configure it to work like Windows, and instead I made it a point to give natural scrolling a try for at least a while before making up my mind as to whether to keep it or lose it. While giving it a try, I was surprised to see that it was very easy for me to adjust to it, despite the fact that I have been using the unnatural Windows scrolling mode for nearly 30 years. (Ever since the mouse wheel became a thing.) I found that natural scrolling was indeed... natural. So, I kept using it, and I became addicted to it. Ever since then, I always have to configure natural scrolling on any Windows machine that I get my hands on before I can start using that machine.

For decades, Windows has been so poor that it did not offer any user interface through which a novice user can change the mouse wheel scrolling mode. To do that you had to edit the registry, and the setting you had to modify was a machine setting, so you would be affecting the mouse wheel mode for all users, not just for yourself. This is unbelievably lame, but hey, that's Windows, we are totally used to lame.

As of Windows 11, update 24H2 which came out in late 2024, there is now support for switching to natural mouse wheel scrolling as a regular user setting; however, this setting is not necessarily observed by software that accesses the mouse via low-level APIs such as DirectX; thus, you may change the setting, and you may enjoy natural mouse wheel scrolling on all of your regular Windows applications, but if you try to play a game, you will find that the wheel works the wrong way in the game, and there is no way to work around that.

So, until all games are updated to respect this new Windows setting, we still have to use the good old registry hack, which is apparently applied at the driver level, and is therefore respected by all software.

There exists a procedure for finding the specific mouse device that you are using, and modifying the wheel mode of only that device, but it is finicky, so we will be skipping that procedure and modifying the setting for all mouse devices that are currently connected to the computer, or have ever been connected. If a new mouse is connected to the system, the procedure will need to be repeated.

Luckily, I do not have any contractual obligations to give warnings regarding the alleged dangers of modifying the registry; so, without further ado, here is what you need to do in order to configure natural scrolling under Windows:

  • Open up RegEdit, and navigate to Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\HID
  • Search for values named FlipFlopWheel. (Do not forget to check the "Search in subtree" checkbox.)
  • For each value you find, if the data is 0, change the data to 1.
  • Restart Windows. (Logging out and back in will not work, because remember, this is a Windows-wide setting, not a per-user setting.)

Cover image: Artwork by michael.gr based on original mouse-15887 by Arkthus from the Noun Project
